lines.text: A seventy-year-old man has just returned from Bangladesh. He is admitted with a high temperature and persistent bloody diarrhoea, and sigmoidoscopy shows a grossly abnormal rectal mucosa. What is the likely diagnosis?
This seventy-year-old traveller has just come home from Bangladesh.
He looks sweaty and miserable, clutching his tummy.
The thermometer is burning. He has a high fever.
The sigmoidoscope shows a raw, grossly abnormal rectal mucosa. The sigmoid colon is a favourite site.
The stowaway on his suitcase is Entamoeba histolytica, caught from contaminated food and water.
Remember: fever and bloody diarrhoea after travel point to amoebic dysentery.
A seventy-five-year-old woman has had difficulty swallowing for four months. Now she has difficulty swallowing even fluids. Of note, she is a regular smoker. What is the likely diagnosis?
This seventy-five-year-old woman cannot even swallow her tea.
Her dysphagia has grown over four months. First solids, and now even fluids get stuck.
(sigh) A tumour is clamping her food pipe tighter and tighter.
And she is a regular smoker. Tobacco and alcohol excess are linked to squamous cell carcinoma.
In general, cancer in the upper two-thirds is squamous cell carcinoma, and in the lower third it is adenocarcinoma.
Remember: progressive dysphagia, even to fluids, in an older smoker means oesophageal carcinoma.
